group.title: Exam skills
group.blurb: How to take the exam, not just what Dutch is. Sentence patterns you can lean on, what to say when a word deserts you, the linking words that lift an answer, getting u and je right, and the tactics and traps for each of the five papers.

topics.title: Sentence frames that always work
topics.summary: A small set of skeletons you can fill with any words. Under exam pressure a frame you can say without thinking beats grammar you have to work out.

blocks.body: On the speaking paper you get about a minute per answer and no second try. There is no time to assemble a sentence from rules. What gets you through is a **pattern you already own**, with a gap to drop today's words into.

blocks.title: Learn five, not fifty
blocks.body: Pick the five frames below that fit the tasks you find hardest, say them out loud until they are automatic, and you will never start an answer with silence again.
For any picture task, these three sentences in this order already make a passing answer. Add detail only once the skeleton is out of your mouth.

items.note: the safest opening in the whole exam

items.nl: Links staat ... en rechts zie ik ...
items.en: On the left there is ... and on the right I see ...

items.nl: Op de voorgrond is iemand aan het ...
items.note: aan het + base form for an action in progress
for a guess about place, season or time

sections.heading: Giving an opinion and a reason

blocks.body: Every choice task and most writing tasks want an opinion plus a reason. This frame covers both and signals structure at the same time.

blocks.title: Mention the option you did not pick
blocks.body: It costs one sentence and shows you can handle a comparison, which is exactly what the task is testing.
For a story task, these four joints carry you through three pictures without pausing to plan.

blocks.title: Pick one tense and stay in it
blocks.body: Past or present, either is accepted. Switching halfway costs more marks than choosing the simpler one and sticking to it.
For the video tasks and for the writing paper, these do the practical work: making a request, proposing a time, and closing politely.

items.en: Could you help me with that?

key_takeaways: Op de foto zie ik ... opens any picture task safely.
Ik kies voor ... want ... plus ten eerste and ten tweede covers any choice task.
Op het eerste plaatje, daarna, uiteindelijk carries a three-part story.
Learn five frames by heart rather than thirty you half remember.
A frame you can say without thinking beats grammar you have to work out.

exercises.prompt: The safest way to start describing a photo: Op de foto ___ ik een supermarkt.
exercises.explain: Op de foto zie ik is the standard opening.

exercises.prompt: Structure your reasons: ___ eerste is het goedkoper.
exercises.explain: Ten eerste and ten tweede are the clearest way to signal structure.

exercises.prompt: Someone is paying right now: Een vrouw is ___ het betalen.
exercises.explain: Aan het plus the base form describes an action in progress.

exercises.prompt: Which opening works for any picture task?
exercises.explain: Op de foto zie ik is the frame to start every picture answer with.

exercises.prompt: You have to choose between two options. Which closes your answer best?
options: Daarom kies ik voor de fiets.
exercises.explain: Daarom plus your choice is a clean, structured ending.

exercises.prompt: Which set of words is for telling a three-picture story?
options: ik wil graag, mag ik, zou u
exercises.explain: Those are the sequencing joints a story needs.

exercises.prompt: Why learn frames rather than more grammar rules for the speaking paper?
options: There is no time to build a sentence from rules under a one-minute timer.
exercises.explain: With about a minute and no retry, an automatic pattern is what gets you through.

exercises.prompt: Say: In the photo I see a busy station.
exercises.explain: Starting with Op de foto pushes the verb to slot two and the subject behind it.

exercises.prompt: Propose a time politely: ___ woensdag u goed uit?
exercises.explain: Komt ... u goed uit? is the standard way to ask whether a time suits.

exercises.prompt: What should you do after saying your opening frame?
options: Stop, because the frame is the answer.
Add detail, then an opinion or a guess.
Repeat the frame with different words.
Switch to English for the details.
exercises.explain: The frame buys you a safe start; the marks come from what you add to it.

topics.title: When you get stuck
topics.summary: What to say when a word deserts you, you did not catch the question, or your mind goes blank. Silence scores nothing; these sentences score something and buy you time.

blocks.body: A missing word is a small problem. **Saying nothing is a big one.** An answer that works around the gap still earns marks; an empty recording earns none. Everything on this page exists to keep you talking.

blocks.title: Freezing on one word
blocks.body: Learners often stop dead because they cannot remember a single noun. The examiner is marking whether you can communicate, not whether you know that noun. Describe it and move on.

sections.heading: Describing a word you cannot remember

blocks.body: Dutch has ready-made ways to talk around a word. Any of these turns a blank into a full sentence.

items.nl: Het is een ding waarmee je ...
items.en: It is a thing you use to ...

items.nl: Hoe zeg je dat in het Nederlands?
items.en: How do you say that in Dutch?

items.nl: Ik weet het woord niet, maar ...
items.en: I do not know the word, but ...

items.note: om te plus the base form

items.nl: Ik weet het woord niet, maar het is een ding waarmee je brood snijdt.
items.en: I do not know the word, but it is a thing you use to cut bread.

items.nl: Het is een soort jas, maar dunner.
items.en: It is a kind of coat, but thinner.

blocks.title: This is a real skill, not a cheat
blocks.body: Talking around a missing word is something fluent speakers do constantly in a second language. Examiners recognise it as competence, not as failure.
Dutch has its own filler sounds. Using them is far better than an English *um*, and much better than dead air.

items.note: a whole sentence of thinking time
for restarting a sentence that went wrong
allowed, and better than trailing off

blocks.title: Restarting is allowed
blocks.body: If a sentence collapses halfway, say `Ik bedoel ...` and say it again properly. A clean second attempt reads better than a broken first one left hanging.

sections.heading: When you did not catch it

blocks.body: Asking someone to repeat is normal, polite Dutch, and on the conversation tasks it is often the correct thing to do. Note the difference between not hearing and not understanding.

rows: Could you say that more slowly?
Ik heb u niet goed verstaan.
I did not catch what you said.
the sound did not reach you
you heard it but the meaning is unclear

blocks.title: verstaan and begrijpen are not the same
blocks.body: `verstaan` is about catching the sound, `begrijpen` is about getting the meaning. Saying `Ik begrijp u niet` to someone who simply spoke too quietly sends the wrong message.

sections.heading: If your mind goes completely blank

blocks.body: Fall back to the simplest true sentence you can make about the topic, then build from there. A plain correct sentence is worth far more than an ambitious broken one.

items.nl: Dat weet ik niet precies, maar ik denk dat ...
items.en: I do not know exactly, but I think that ...

items.nl: Daar heb ik geen ervaring mee, maar ...
items.en: I have no experience with that, but ...

items.nl: Ik vind het een moeilijke vraag. Voor mij is het zo: ...
items.en: I find that a difficult question. For me it is like this: ...

blocks.title: Simple and correct beats ambitious and broken
blocks.body: At A2 you are not rewarded for complexity. Short, clear, finished sentences score well.

key_takeaways: Silence scores nothing, so always say something.
Talk around a missing word with Het is een soort ... or Het is een ding waarmee je ...
Even denken buys you a moment and sounds natural.
verstaan is about hearing, begrijpen is about understanding.
A simple correct sentence beats an ambitious broken one.

exercises.prompt: You cannot recall the word for a bread knife. Het is een ___ waarmee je brood snijdt.
exercises.explain: Het is een ding waarmee je ... turns a blank into a full sentence.

exercises.prompt: Buy yourself a moment: ___ denken ...
exercises.explain: Even denken is the most useful filler in the exam.

exercises.prompt: You did not hear the question. Sorry, kunt u dat ___?
exercises.explain: Kunt u dat herhalen? is the standard polite request to repeat.

exercises.prompt: The examiner spoke too quietly and you caught nothing. Which is right?
options: Ik heb u niet goed verstaan.
exercises.explain: Verstaan is about catching the sound. Begrijpen would say the meaning was unclear.

exercises.prompt: You have forgotten a noun completely. What is the best move?
options: Stay silent until you remember it.
Say the English word and carry on.
Describe the thing in Dutch and keep going.
exercises.explain: Describing it keeps you scoring. Silence scores nothing.

exercises.prompt: Your sentence collapses halfway through. What do you do?
options: Stop and wait for the next question.
Say Ik bedoel ... and say it again properly.
exercises.explain: Restarting cleanly is allowed and reads better than leaving it hanging.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means you heard the words but not the meaning?
exercises.explain: Begrijpen is about meaning, verstaan is about sound.

exercises.prompt: Say: I do not know the word, but it is a kind of bag.
exercises.explain: Naming the gap and then describing it is a complete, scoring answer.

exercises.prompt: Check you understood correctly: ___ u dat ik morgen moet komen?
exercises.explain: Bedoelt u ...? checks your understanding without stopping the conversation.

exercises.prompt: Why is a short correct sentence better than a long broken one at A2?
options: A2 rewards clear communication, not complexity.
The examiner stops listening after ten words.
exercises.explain: At A2 you are marked on getting the message across clearly.

topics.title: Linking words that lift a pass
topics.summary: The small words that turn a list of sentences into an argument. Structure is marked on both the writing and the speaking paper, and these are the cheapest marks on offer.

blocks.body: Two answers can contain the same facts and score differently. The one that **signals its structure** reads as organised; the one that does not reads as a list. These words are the signals, and there are only about a dozen to learn.

blocks.title: Cheapest marks in the exam
blocks.body: Adding `ten eerste`, `bovendien` and `daarom` to an answer you were going to give anyway takes no extra vocabulary and no extra grammar.

items.en: what is more, on top of that

items.nl: Ten eerste is het goedkoper. Ten tweede is het sneller.
items.en: Firstly it is cheaper. Secondly it is faster.
items.note: note the inversion: ten eerste fills slot one, so the verb comes next

blocks.title: Forgetting the inversion
blocks.body: `Ten eerste` and `bovendien` fill the first slot of the sentence, so the verb has to come straight after: `Bovendien **is** het gezonder`, not `Bovendien het is gezonder`.

rows: usually fills slot one, so inversion
blocks.note: want and omdat mean the same thing, but only omdat moves the verb.

items.nl: Ik ga met de fiets, want het is dichtbij.
items.en: I go by bike, because it is close by.

items.nl: Ik ga met de fiets omdat het dichtbij is.
items.en: I go by bike because it is close by.
items.note: omdat sends is to the end

items.nl: Het is dichtbij. Daarom ga ik met de fiets.
items.en: It is close by. That is why I go by bike.

items.note: sends the verb to the end
Het regent, maar ik ga toch.

items.nl: De trein is sneller, maar de fiets is goedkoper.
items.en: The train is faster, but the bike is cheaper.

items.nl: Hoewel het duur is, koop ik het.
items.en: Although it is expensive, I am buying it.
items.note: verb to the end, then inversion after the comma

items.nl: Aan de andere kant is de trein comfortabeler.
items.en: On the other hand the train is more comfortable.

items.note: the single most useful filler word

blocks.title: Hedging is not weakness
blocks.body: `Misschien`, `waarschijnlijk` and `ik denk dat` let you say something about a picture you are not sure of without being wrong. On a picture task you cannot be wrong if you hedge.

key_takeaways: Structure is marked, and these words are the cheapest way to show it.
Ten eerste, ten tweede, bovendien and tot slot order your points.
want changes nothing, omdat sends the verb to the end, daarom causes inversion.
Bovendien and daarom fill slot one, so the verb must follow them straight away.
Hedging with misschien or ik denk dat lets you guess safely.

exercises.prompt: Signal your first reason: ___ eerste is het goedkoper.
exercises.explain: Ten eerste is the clearest way to open a list of reasons.

exercises.prompt: Bovendien ___ het gezonder. Which verb form fits the gap?
exercises.explain: Bovendien fills slot one, so the verb comes straight after it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has the right word order?
exercises.explain: Bovendien takes the first slot, so the verb must follow immediately.

exercises.prompt: Which word means because but changes nothing about word order?
exercises.explain: Want joins two equal clauses, so nothing moves.

exercises.prompt: Ik ga met de fiets ___ het dichtbij is. Which fits?
exercises.explain: The verb is at the end of the clause, which is what omdat does.

exercises.prompt: You want to add a contrasting point. Which opens it best?
exercises.explain: Aan de andere kant signals that a contrast is coming.

exercises.prompt: Give an example: Ik eet graag Nederlands eten, ___ stamppot.
exercises.explain: Bijvoorbeeld introduces an example and fills space usefully.

exercises.prompt: Hedge a guess about a photo: ___ mij is het zaterdagmiddag.
exercises.explain: Volgens mij lets you guess without being wrong.

exercises.prompt: Say: That is why I go by bike. Start with Daarom.
exercises.explain: Daarom fills slot one, so the verb comes next and the subject follows it.

exercises.prompt: Why do linking words earn marks even when the content is unchanged?
options: Structure is one of the things the paper is marked on.
They count towards the word total.
exercises.explain: Both the writing and the speaking paper assess how well organised the answer is.

topics.title: u or je, and how to open and close
topics.summary: Picking the wrong level of politeness is marked, and it is easy to avoid. Who gets u, who gets je, and the fixed openings and closings that have to match.

blocks.body: Ask one question: **do I know this person, and are we equals?** If yes, `je`. If they are a stranger in an official role, or clearly older, `u`.

rows: Shop assistant you do not know
stranger, though je is creeping in
A neighbour who introduced themselves by first name

blocks.title: When genuinely unsure, pick u
blocks.body: Being slightly too formal is a tiny misstep. Being too familiar with an official is a real one. The exam will not punish you for politeness.
`u` always takes the **-t** form of the verb, even though it can mean one person or several.

items.en: What would you like to drink?

blocks.title: Mixing u and je in one conversation
blocks.body: Once you have chosen, stay with it. Starting with `u` and sliding into `je` halfway is noticeable and costs you on the register criterion.
On the writing paper the opening and the closing are a **pair**. A formal opening with a casual sign-off is a clear error, and it is one of the easiest marks to lose.

blocks.title: Geachte heer/mevrouw with Groetjes
blocks.body: This is the mismatch examiners see most. If you opened with `Geachte`, you must close with `Met vriendelijke groet`.

blocks.title: Always sign your name
blocks.body: A note or email with no name underneath is marked as incomplete, however good the Dutch is.
Dutch has its own phone opening. You do not say `ik ben`.

items.note: the standard way to say who you are

blocks.title: Saying Ik ben Sara on the phone
blocks.body: It is understandable but marks you out instantly as a learner. `U spreekt met ...` or `Met ...` is what Dutch speakers say.

key_takeaways: Stranger in an official role takes u, someone you know and are equal with takes je.
When unsure, choose u. Too formal is a small error, too familiar is a real one.
u always takes the -t form of the verb.
Geachte pairs with Met vriendelijke groet; Hoi pairs with Groetjes.
On the phone say U spreekt met ..., never Ik ben ...

exercises.prompt: At the doctor's desk: ___ u een moment?
exercises.explain: u takes the -t form, and both hebt and heeft are accepted.

exercises.prompt: On the phone, say who you are: ___ spreekt met Sara Nowak.
exercises.explain: U spreekt met is the standard Dutch phone opening.

exercises.prompt: You are writing to the gemeente. Which pair is right?
exercises.explain: A formal opening has to be matched by a formal closing.

exercises.prompt: A colleague your own age invites you for a drink. Which do you use?
options: jullie, because it is a group
exercises.explain: A colleague of your own age takes je, and register is marked.

exercises.prompt: You are not sure whether to use u or je. What is the safer choice?
options: u, because being too familiar is the bigger error
Avoid both by using the person's name
Switch between them to cover both
exercises.explain: Slightly too formal is a small misstep; too familiar with an official is a real one.

exercises.prompt: Which is wrong on the phone?
exercises.explain: Dutch uses U spreekt met or Met, never Ik ben, to open a call.

exercises.prompt: Close a formal email: Met vriendelijke ___,
exercises.explain: Met vriendelijke groet is the standard formal sign-off.

exercises.prompt: Close a note to a friend: ___,
exercises.explain: Groetjes or Groeten matches an informal opening.

exercises.prompt: Ask politely whether someone can help you. (use u)
exercises.explain: A question puts the verb first, and u takes the -t form.

exercises.prompt: What happens if you start a conversation with u and switch to je halfway?
options: It is noticeable and costs marks on register.
It shows range and scores higher.
Only switching from je to u is a problem.
exercises.explain: Once you have chosen a level of politeness, stay with it.

topics.title: Tactics, paper by paper
topics.summary: What to actually do on the day: where the marks are on each of the five papers, the traps that cost people a pass, and how to spend the time.

sections.heading: The one habit that covers every paper

blocks.body: **Answer the question that was asked.** The commonest reason for losing marks at A2 is not bad Dutch, it is a good answer to a slightly different question. Before you write or speak, check what was actually requested.

blocks.title: Count the asks
blocks.body: Most tasks ask for two or three specific things. Count them, then check them off as you answer. The writing paper is marked on exactly this.

items.en: Then read the text knowing what you are hunting for.
items.note: saves the most time of anything here

items.nl: The answer is in the text
items.en: Never pick an option because it sounds sensible in real life.
One small negative flips the whole meaning of a sentence.

items.nl: Do not stop at an unknown word
items.en: Read the whole sentence. The meaning usually survives one missing word.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

items.nl: Read the question before the audio starts
items.en: You get a moment. Use it to know what to listen for.

items.nl: You will not catch every word
items.en: Nobody does. Listen for the one piece of information asked for.
Practise hearing prices, clock times and dates specifically.
Chasing it means missing the next sentence too.
A guess costs nothing and sometimes lands.

blocks.title: Freezing on one missed word
blocks.body: Learners often stop listening while they try to work out a word they missed, and lose the rest of the clip. Let it go immediately and stay with the speaker.

items.en: This is the first thing marked, before any grammar.
Geachte with Met vriendelijke groet, Hoi with Groetjes.
An unsigned note is marked as incomplete.
Three clear sentences beat one ambitious one that falls apart.
On a form, a Dutch postcode is four digits and two letters, and dates run day, month, year.

blocks.title: Write the checklist in the margin
blocks.body: Jot the asks down before you start, then tick them off. It takes twenty seconds and is the difference between a pass and a near miss.

items.en: Op de foto zie ik ... buys you a safe opening.

items.nl: Keep going for the whole time
items.en: A short answer cannot score well, however correct it is.

items.nl: Simple and finished beats complex and broken
items.en: Do not attempt sentences you cannot land.
You are marked on being understood, not on sounding Dutch.

items.nl: If you dry up, describe or hedge
items.en: Misschien ... , Ik denk dat ... , Het is een soort ...

blocks.title: Stopping after one sentence
blocks.body: You have about a minute per answer. Finishing in ten seconds leaves most of the marks unclaimed, even if what you said was perfect.

items.nl: It is about how things work here
items.en: Not about opinions or your own country.

items.nl: Think about which body does what
items.en: gemeente, UWV, SVB, Belastingdienst, IND each have their own job.

items.nl: Pick the normal Dutch thing to do
items.en: When unsure, choose the ordinary, practical, direct option.
Learn who does what rather than this year's amounts.

blocks.body: Practical things that are easy to forget and expensive to get wrong.

items.en: You will not be admitted without it.
Being late can cost you the whole sitting.
You can pass them one at a time and retake only what you failed.
Many people pass on a second attempt at one paper. It is not a verdict on you.

blocks.title: Check your own booking details with DUO
blocks.body: Fees, booking and the exact rules change. This page teaches technique; DUO is the authority on arrangements.

key_takeaways: Answer the question that was actually asked, and count how many things it asks for.
Reading: read the questions first, and watch for niet and geen.
Listening: let a missed word go immediately rather than losing the next sentence.
Writing: cover every point, match your opening and closing, and sign it.
Speaking: start with a frame and keep going for the full time.
Never leave a blank, because a wrong answer costs nothing.

exercises.prompt: What is the most useful thing to do first on the reading paper?
options: Read the questions before the text.
exercises.explain: Knowing what you are hunting for saves more time than anything else.

exercises.prompt: You miss a word in the middle of a listening clip. What do you do?
options: Let it go and keep listening.
Ask for the clip to be replayed.
Write down what it sounded like.
exercises.explain: Chasing a missed word costs you the sentences that follow.

exercises.prompt: What is marked first on the writing paper?
options: Whether you covered every point the task asked for.
exercises.explain: Coverage comes before language on the A2 writing paper.

exercises.prompt: Your speaking answer is correct but only ten seconds long. What happens?
options: Full marks, since it was correct.
It cannot score well, because too little was said.
It is marked as a pass automatically.
exercises.explain: You have about a minute, and a short answer leaves most marks unclaimed.

exercises.prompt: You do not know an answer on a multiple-choice paper. What should you do?
options: Guess, because a wrong answer costs nothing.
exercises.explain: There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

exercises.prompt: Which small words most often flip the meaning of a reading sentence?
exercises.explain: A single negative changes the whole sentence, and it is a classic trap.

exercises.prompt: On KNM, you are unsure which body handles something. What is the best approach?
options: Pick the one with the longest name.
Think about which organisation does that job.
Choose the answer closest to your own country.
exercises.explain: KNM tests how the system works, so reason from what each body is for.

exercises.prompt: Does a noticeable accent lower your speaking mark?
options: Yes, pronunciation is the main criterion.
No, you are marked on being understood.
exercises.explain: An accent is fine. Being hard to understand is the problem, and that is different.

exercises.prompt: You failed one paper and passed the others. What now?
options: You have to sit all five again.
You retake only the paper you failed.
You wait a year before any retake.
exercises.explain: The papers are booked and passed separately.

exercises.prompt: Before you start writing, count how many things the task ___ for.
exercises.explain: Most tasks ask for two or three specific points, and coverage is marked first.
